gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX S2000 shares one 1,500 W (12.5 A) limit across all five of its 120 V sockets, or that Anker's own S2000 page warns that 'a 1,500 W microwave plus a fridge compressor surge can exceed comfortable headroom'. That rules the S2000 out for a typical outage kit of a kitchen appliance plus a fridge, while the $899 BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 ran 2,028 Wh at up to 2,600 W in APH Networks' test.
standout_why: I compared against gearjunkie.com (cited), outagereadyhq.com (cited), wattpowerstation.com (cited) and powerstations.reviews/prices (cited). GearJunkie already says the S2000 is 'capped at a continuous 1,500 W', and ChatGPT's answer warned that the S2000's output is lower than the 2,400 W models. So the 1,500 W limit itself is not new. What none of them has: the limit is shared by all five sockets (ESS News: '1,500 W total, 12.5 A'), Anker's own warning about a microwave plus a fridge compressor, and any statement on how boost modes behave. APH measured that the Elite 200 V2's Power Lifting mode stops at 2,600 W: two hair dryers spiking to 3,140 W shut the unit down. OutageReadyHQ and Watt Power Station give no output, outlet or boost details at all. powerstations.reviews lists only prices. I could not load the Popular Mechanics page.
decides: This keeps the S2000 out of the general 'best 2000 W' pick. Its own maker says it is meant for fridge and bedside backup, not for kitchen loads on top of a fridge. Anker's US store also shows $999.99 today, not the $699.99 ChatGPT quoted, which removes its price advantage. The pick should go to a 2,200–2,600 W unit. The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 at $899 on BLUETTI's store today has the best-documented output and capacity (APH: 2,028 Wh usable, 97.8% of rated). The cheaper Dabbsson 2000L and Pecron E2400LFP remain value options, but I could not open either maker page to confirm their outputs.
